Stirred and strained, the Behind the Scenes donated a minty herbal, roasted vegetal, and smoke bouquet to the nose. The security take-off is here, and the answer isn't more AI. It's engineering. I gave a talk at AI DevCon New York about patching the planet with Nix and agents, how I got through the last round of security incidents without losing any sleep, and a bonus round on loops, back pressure and property-based testing.

Everyone at the conference spent two days hearing about how to build software faster with factories. Cool. I wanted to talk about something different: how do you respond to security incidents faster? It turns out that if you optimise for incident response times, your build times speed up too. Here's the talk, written up properly, with the slides broken out and chapter links at the bottom if you want to jump to a specific part.

It turns out the answer for AI is engineering.

two weeks ago was pretty wild, huh?

OpenCode got breached. Then the Prime Minister of Japan was tweeting at everyone to go and update PHP.

Next thing you know, there's a vulnerability in an HTTP stack that lets anyone remotely turn off a running server. Then a 12-year-old GitLab flaw that led to remote code execution on self-managed servers. Ouch.

And it turns out the answer to life, the universe, and everything isn't 42. It's 4. A certificate authority had a key that should have been a 116-digit number, and it was just 4. Anyone who could guess it could forge HTTPS certificates for any website.

The number 4 opens all doors on the internet.

So we started wondering: is it time to turn the internet off yet?

You've probably seen the graph of GitHub pull requests going quadratic, and GitHub having availability issues because of it. That's agent take-off. Below is the security version of that: the security take-off.

I'm putting it to you that this is the start of the new normal. You could argue it's a bump in the road, and once all the software has been patched, things will calm down. Maybe. But agents are writing software now; agents were trained on existing code, and existing code is full of these vulnerabilities.

you'll need more inferencing than your attackers

Unfortunately, cyber is only going to accelerate from here. It's going to get really weird, because I suspect you're going to need more inferencing capacity than your attackers to stay secure.

Think about the companies right now saying, "oh no, we can only do a $100-a-month token budget per employee." Yeah, no. As soon as you publish any code on GitHub, someone with racks of inferencing hardware will autonomously scan it and then autonomously make tool calls to exploit what they find. That's the new state of normal.

why do we have open-source dependencies?

Almost a year ago I wrote a blog post asking why we even have open-source libraries. I got grilled to hell on Hacker News for it, but every day that goes by it becomes more true.

We had open-source libraries because code was precious. It was hard to write, so we concentrated it into libraries to make reuse easy. We also did it to make hiring easier: React was famously a play by Facebook to standardise frontend development so they could hire for it. We optimised our practices for humans, and I don't think we need libraries anymore.

I'm not saying you should go and vibe-code your own cryptography. If you're a cryptographer, please do. I'm not. There's still going to be a trusted base and a trusted core. But think about your supply chain. How much time do you spend on Dependabot updates? How much time do you spend on incident response because a Dependabot update was compromised, because the upstream author was compromised? We're already losing time, all because the prior was that writing software was hard.

It's been a year, and I don't use much open source anymore. Sure, I use the Linux kernel, DNS servers like BIND, and the lower-level stuff. But once I get into higher-level code, I just prompt the agent for what I want. It feels very unnatural at first. If it's small and well-specified, like a command-line argument parser, you could take that dependency, or you could have Claude build it in a loop.

Something magical happens when you do: it's built for your use case, and you don't need to get someone on GitHub to merge your pull request. It turns out that if you have to tool call a human, that's not AGI.

So the best you can do is either generate it first-party, or vendor the open-source software and check it into your repo so the agent can modify and extend it. That's one approach. Today I want to show you a different one.

patching is perceived to be hard

I'm calling it patch the planet. Patching is perceived to be hard, but it doesn't have to be. What makes it hard? Say you want to patch something on GitHub. You have to figure out how that software builds, learn its toolchain, and set up a new CI job just for that one thing. You do that per language, and every open-source library has a different build toolchain. Then once you've patched it, you need to host it in an artifact repo, and now you're thinking about artifact tokens. We make things needlessly complex.

There's been a solution for a long time: Nix. It's been around since 2003, and I've used it for years. You might have heard that Nix sucks. It does. There's no silver bullet. The most common complaint is that it's hard to use. It was. Agents know how to drive towards an outcome, so you just need to know that Nix exists, then prompt the agent: I want Nix here. The same goes for Bazel and Buck2. Talk to any eng leader, and they've got a story about nearly getting fired after staffing a team of five to introduce one of these, and then spending forever upskilling every developer. That's no longer true. You can now use highly complex, high-powered tools simply. You just have to know they exist, and you have to falsify your priors.

one source of truth

The demo is up on my GitHub as nix-demo below. Clone it down and have a look, because there are some interesting things in there. I use devenv, which is a nice gentle introduction to Nix. You define your packages and services in Nix, and that one file generates your developer laptops, your CI/CD, your agent sandboxes and your production Docker images.

See where I'm going? A single source of truth. How many people are spinning up teams right now to figure out agent sandboxes, and are they just duplicating environments? I'd bet that at some of your companies the laptop setup isn't reproducible: onboard a new employee or lose a laptop, and it's 48 hours to rebuild the developer environment. Then there's drift in CI/CD, so it works on your computer but CI says it doesn't. The agent sandbox is another source of drift. And finally, you say it's all done, but your software increment doesn't work in the production Docker image.

Interestingly, the Docker images Nix produces are incredibly efficient. Docker basically stacks file-system layers on top of each other and squashes them. Nix is a graph, and it uses that graph to build a very optimised image.

a git that cannot force push

Imagine I'm a new engineer with a brand new computer, onboarding into the company; all I need to do is change my working directory to the source code checkout.

My globally installed git is 2.54, but I cd into the project, and I'm onboarded.

Think nvm or a Python version manager, but for all of your operating-system dependencies, including across the FFI boundaries; it goes past the programming language.

After changing my working directory git is 2.55. What's so special about this version of git? It's not just a newer version.

This version of git doesn't support force push. I've monkey-patched it for my agent sandboxes, my local engineering laptops, and everywhere else I use git. It's a single source of git, so anything that needs git as a transitive dependency also gets my patched version.

The best way to stop a model from doing something is to remove its ability to do it.

How do you stop an agent from force pushing? It hill-climbs toward its goal and does destructive things along the way. When that causes incidents, remove the capability from the underlying system. I use this trick all over the place, and sometimes the best way is to monkey-patch the system underneath.

Those of you from my generation will remember patch files. Open source used to be distributed as a collection of patch files. The idea that everything must be merged upstream on GitHub was never part of open source. This is how we used to do software development. Here I have a closure that defines git, plus my custom patches.

How did I get the custom patches? I asked Claude: Can you please use Nix and create a custom overlay that removes force push? Done. Now a set of Unix patches is applied to git automatically whenever I'm in that environment. And it's not just that environment. It could be Docker, or a production host, wherever you like.

This one little pattern makes the entire world patchable. You're no longer waiting on someone upstream to merge a bug fix. You just route around it.

patch the planet

There's no hidden magic and no skeletons in the closet. I import the overlay and Nix handles the rest. You might think mise is good software. It's not; it's a package manager like Homebrew. Does it have this level of functionality? Nix lets you patch anything, including the operating system kernel, and then deploy that custom version across your fleet.

About a month before the incidents, I wrote about what happens when there's a critical fault in OpenSSL. You can update OpenSSL. Cool. But what about when it's a transitive dependency? OpenSSL is used by Nginx and Postgres, so it isn't just a matter of patching OpenSSL itself. That's why we never patched things manually. With a single source of truth for OpenSSL, you apply a monkey patch just like I did with git, and Nix recompiles the world. Every transitive dependency gets the custom version.

Nix has good caching and remote builders, similar to Bazel, so this doesn't mean compiling forever. CI compiles the software once, validates it, and publishes it to the cache, and your developer environments and sandboxes download from it. Simple.

So the question I want to put to you is: how much productivity did you lose two weeks ago during those security incidents?

I didn't lose any sleep, folks, because I have a single source of truth. I opened Claude and asked whether my fleet was affected.

It said yes, and from there it applied the monkey patches it needed and updated the refs, dependencies, and pins. Because everything flows from that source of truth, the transitive dependencies recompiled automatically. Done. I'm living the nirvana life over here, and you could be too. You just have to know this exists.

the AGENTS.md reminder trick

There was one cute trick I did. After the "am I affected?" prompt, I had some temporary monkey patches in place, similar to the git overlay. So I issued another prompt: update the AGENTS.md, and in seven days' time, get rid of my patches.

Instead of creating a Jira ticket, I added a reminder to my AGENTS.md. The next developer or agent to pick up that machine automatically did the housekeeping, and backed out the monkey patches and pins because upstream had been fixed. This is the easiest security maintenance I've ever done. Every time there's a security issue, I use these two tricks.

If you optimise for this, your security incident response gets faster, and your productivity for factories and everything else gets faster too. The answer for AI is engineering.

root, but only in a sandbox

I had ten minutes left, so I did a bonus round on loops. Everyone has their own way of doing loop engineering. There are no best practices, and my way is very different from Steve's. Surprise: mine involves Nix, which has a very powerful testing primitive.

When I run my loops, I give my agents sudo. They run as root. Would you do that on an Ubuntu machine? Hell no. But a throwaway Nix developer machine has some unique properties. I can run these loops with sudo, which lets the agent inspect everything from the database to the journals, and it's safe because I designed the operating environment for it.

Here's why that matters. Nix has a testing framework called the NixOS test. Imagine two web servers with a load balancer in front, on different network VLANs. How would you normally test that? It would be really hard. With Nix, you define what you need; it creates all the machines, and you can assert that your network rules hold.

When I run my loops, the entire operating system, the fleet and the higher-tier stack are all under test, integrated from day one. When the agent finishes a unit of work, I test it on exactly what would be production infrastructure, because the infrastructure is defined as code. I can deploy that increment somewhere as a preview environment. Run production from Nix flakes, spin up something identical to production, test the hell out of it, and if it's green, it will be correct when you apply that flake to production.

Having said all that: do not run agents with Nix as root on production hosts, and do not connect agents to production databases. Ever. If you need to reproduce something, build a workflow that duplicates the database and restrict the heck out of outbound network access. Dev parity really is equal at this point. One source of truth, one way up.

don't let the loop close

Ralph was never just about loops. It was about stopping the loop from closing on bad code. The loop generates code, commits it, compiles it, and so on. The best way to stop it closing on bad output is deterministic checks. These aren't skills. This is engineering again.

You can block a git push if the software doesn't compile. That's a pre-commit hook, or prek, and you can engineer a lot of back pressure with hooks. Then add static analysis, such as "this domain must never be coupled to that domain". Say you have an API domain and a SQL domain. You don't want SQL to reference the API. That would normally be an architecture review, but agents are pretty dumb and will do it anyway. Wondering how to solve your code review problems? Engineer away much of the need for code review with checks like these, using static and semantic analysis from your language's language service. There's so much you can do. You just have to ask.

property-based testing

Next, unit tests. The problem with unit tests is that they only test what you specify, so edge cases slip through. That's where property-based testing comes in. It has been around for years, and you should be using it.

Say you have a function that reverses a string, and the implementation is faulty because it doesn't support Unicode or emoji. I never wrote that test, so it slips through. That's a whole category of problems.

With property-based testing, a generator feeds in random strings, emoji, huge strings and long strings, and keeps exploring the state space to check that your property holds. The property here is that reversing a string twice gives you back the original string. And I'm not just talking about reversing strings. I'm talking about properties like "a customer who asks for a refund is only refunded once", across the whole lifecycle and all of your microservices. Properties take some getting used to, but they're really cool.

bombadil and hegel

At Antithesis, validation and verification of software is what we do. We have a library called Bombadil. You should ditch Playwright, folks, and I'm not just talking my book. Bombadil lets you write a property, such as "the user always has the ability to log out". It loads your plain JavaScript or TypeScript application in a web browser and puts it through hell: rotating the screen, changing dimensions, going full screen, and committing every random act of violence it can against your app until the property either holds or fails. When it fails, you get a counterexample: a reproduction of exactly how it failed.

Fun fact: back in February we woke up to find PewDiePie using it, and we still don't know how, because this is academic knowledge, not popular knowledge. Maybe it's in the model weights.

We also have Hegel: a small core library written in Rust, with sugar on top for each programming language. You might know its predecessor, Hypothesis. Same team, same tech, but now we're bringing it to every programming language. Do these two things in your codebase and, beyond solving your patching woes, you'll get a massive uplift across your organisation. They're free. You just have to know they exist and use them.

Traditionally, many of us believe in a world where how hard you work is more important than who you know. I used to subscribe to this idea as both a scientist, who believed that facts about our world are agnostic to who says them, and as an American, who grew up believing that success was a function of how hard you worked, not who you knew.

However I am now feeling a substantial change in AI, specifically in the past five years, where who you know is becoming more important, and what you can do is becoming less important. I am obviously not saying that technical skills don’t matter, or that you cannot be successful without being well connected. Technical skills are still important and make or break your career. But I am noticing a trend. To assign arbitrary numbers, I would say that five years ago, success was 75% your skills and 25% who you knew. Now, it is maybe 55% skills and 45% who you know.

Riffing on the work started with Ask Rands, I’ve been spending the days before the holiday seasons polishing existing features while also building some new ones for the blog.

Briefs

If you’ve been watching the RSS feed for the past week, you’ve seen an increase in the number of posts. During the last major redesign of the site, Alex and I created a post type called Excerpts — the idea was a new post type for links and small bits of content. I posted many of these, but then stopped… I don’t know why. Essay-length pieces seemed to be more my jam?

With my robot-friends, I’ve built a new post type called Briefs, which include photos, text, songs, and links. Yes, I know… hello 2005… but I wanted a path to post more frequently on smaller topics, so now we have Briefs.

Tags

Building Briefs revealed another feature that was popular, I don’t know, two decades ago? Tags. Yeah, Web 2.0.

In my head at redesign time, WordPress Categories were tags, but over the years Categories became more defined themes (Management, Product, Tech Life, etc.) than tags. Thanks again to the robots, I’ve added tags to Briefs, as well as all existing posts. There’s a very tight vocabulary to prevent tag-bloat, and you can find a very well-organized list of tags here.

Tags now appear at the bottom of posts. I’ve done some behind-the-scenes wizardry to map Categories to Tags such that I hope you never notice. Holler if you do, and it’s annoying.

How Ask Rands Works

One of the unexpected benefits of the Ask Rands feature is the questions Grumbles has no idea how to answer. He logs these questions and tells me. Every morning. Thanks, Grumbles.

Many readers have asked Grumbles how Ask Rands works. There are two parts:

On WP Engine:

  • On randsinrepose.com, the /ask/ page and the Ask button are part of the site’s theme.
  • A search runs in your browser. Yes, you are downloading a snapshot of every article, then searching. This costs nothing and requires no server. I’m hoping you have not noticed this.

On Railway:

  • A small answer server lives here. This is Grumbles. You send a question to this server, which calls Claude and streams the answer back. Many of you have asked about the Grumbles “voice”. This is the prompt that I provide to Claude as a template for Grumbles’ personality1.
  • Repeated questions are stored and echoed back to reduce cost.
  • All questions, anonymized, are sitting in a small database along with answers which I review daily.
  • The server also enforces spending caps, per-reader limits, and timeouts.

Finally, Cloudflare throws up those “are you a person” checks and does rate limiting.

Since launch, I’ve added the following features to Ask Rands:

  • Contextually aware follow-ups.
  • A smarter “I don’t know” — Grumbles was claiming I covered topics that I didn’t.
  • Reversal detection. If I changed my mind about something, you see both sides of the argument.
  • A bunch of better matches for specific questions.
  • Made it clear that Grumbles doesn’t search my books — just the blog posts where most of the books started.

I’ve been fascinated by the questions being asked. Grumbles highlights gaps in my current writing on preventing gaslighting, dealing with underperformers, absent leadership, and other specific bad cases.

And finally…

Search 2.0

At the top of the least-visited top-level page lives a search box. This is a Web 1.0 dumb as dirt keyword search that I have confirmed you never use. This page has been untouched for years, primarily because I believe most folks look for Rands stuff on Google.

Google AI Overviews decimate traffic — a 50%+ decrease in clicks to the first link. That’s good for Google, but bad for content producers. Here’s the thing: thanks to the robots, you are no longer as dependent on Google for search. Ask Rands and Tags are both features that have been vastly easier to build with the help of the robots, but I don’t think that’s what is going to drive humans to human-produced content.

The voice of Google AI Overviews is the same soulless sound as many of the default robots. You have the same reaction to AI-generated art: this is slop, and I want heart.

My hope is that, because many of the services and tools have been democratized with the help of the robots, content producers can provide you, dear reader, a more compelling experience and more reasons to hang out.

We’ll see.

  1. Here’s an example of that prompt: At most one joke per answer about being a robot, and skip the worn ones: nobody thanking you or asking you, never being invited, unpaid, the Mac Studio, rebooting. Most asides should come from the reader’s situation, not yours.

content:
I am not a believer in glue work1. Processes that can only be sustained by the unrewarded sacrifice of engineers ought to die.

Now that LLMs are writing most of our code, does that free human engineers up to do more glue work? No, it doesn’t. I think glue work is actually less important to companies than it was in the 2010s. Let’s go through four reasons why.

First, AI decreases the amount of coordination needed to ship. The magnifying effect of AI agents means that any single engineer can now take on projects that would previously have needed a small team. A lot of glue work was helping with coordination: booking kickoff and status meetings, passing around internal updates, and so on. A single engineer doesn’t need to do any of that.

Second, engineers in the 2020s require less “careful handling”. In my experience, the most important subcategory of coordination-based glue work was managing difficult people. Many companies have secret gatekeepers: engineers with outsized influence and large egos who will shoot down your project if they feel insufficiently consulted. I’ve written before about how some teams are structurally set up to be gatekeepers, and how some engineers could get by in the 2010s by basically saying no to everything. The end of ZIRP changed all that. Many of the prickliest gatekeepers have been forced out of the industry or coerced into changing their attitude, which reduces the amount of necessary glue work required to ship.

Third, people are hiring fewer juniors. This is probably a bad thing for the industry, but it does also eliminate a big category of glue work. Experienced hires need less hand-holding, so companies don’t need people to quietly volunteer to onboard new hires.

Fourth, write-only reports can be automated with LLMs. A lot of glue work was what I call “proof of work”: writing a report to demonstrate that you’re aware of what your team is doing, or filling in a template to satisfy some legal requirement. This was often work that nobody wanted to do, so it relied on someone volunteering to “be glue”. Now reports like these can be quickly turned out with LLMs. It doesn’t really matter that nobody wants to read LLM text, because the point of these reports was never to be read anyway.

Can LLMs just automate all glue work? Absolutely not. Many engineers are trying to do this out of a kind of manic optimism, but it’s a really bad idea. Write-only reports are one thing, but communicating to other engineers cannot be delegated to an LLM. When you need to check in on the status of a project, or respond to someone else’s ping, or anything like that, you should compose and write the message yourself. Nothing will torch your relationship with other engineers as quickly as making them talk to your Claude Opus instance.

So where does that leave us? More or less where we were in 2024, I think. Avoid at all costs becoming “the glue work person”, let bad processes fail so they can be changed, but be willing to do small amounts of tactical glue work where it can meaningfully contribute to the success of your projects. Most of your time and effort should still be spent on the code: on driving AI agents and aligning them with your company’s values.

  1. Glue work is all the squishy “non-technical” work that goes into building software: making sure teams are talking to each other, writing reports, updating docs, onboarding engineers, and so on. Specifically it’s the parts of that work that are not included in the formal process, and that only really get done if someone volunteers to do it. For more on why I don’t like it, see my 2024 post Glue work considered harmful.

I.

Here’s a fun argument you can use to discredit anyone at any time.

Start by calling them an arrogant fanatic with a totalizing ideology, someone who thinks they personally have solved all problems and can’t possibly learn from anyone who disagrees. If they have friends who agree with them, they’re a cult who collectively work to shelter themselves from any dissenting viewpoint.

Then your victim responds by presenting one hundred notarized affadavits describing times when they have engaged with their critics, spent years studying books by their critics to see what they could learn from them, and even changed their beliefs in response to criticism.

Then you spring the trap: “Ah, but you cherry-picked critics who operate within your worldview, a sort of loyal opposition. You continue to dismiss and exclude genuine critics who challenge your smug assumptions.”

This always works. If your victim protests that they do like and appreciate many critics with worldviews different to theirs, you object that no, those guys are also within the system. You meant a different guy, even further away from their own view. Oh, they read that one too? You meant an even more different guy. Eventually, no matter how cosmopolitan they are, you will reach someone they actually don’t respect - let’s say a Stalinist pedophile who believes the Papacy is a Jewish plot - and then you go ha! I told you that you rejected everyone outside your little bubble!

Everyone has people close to their ideology who they respect, and people far away from it who they don’t respect. Professionally, I work from a tradition of medicalized psychiatry influenced by figures like Kraepelin, Kline, and (sigh) Stahl. When I operate within that tradition - let’s say by prescribing escitalopram to a depressed patient - here are five circles of critics I might consider listening to:

  1. The Colleague: “Instead of prescribing escitalopram, you should prescribe bupropion, which studies show is equally efficacious with fewer side effects.”

  2. The Biopsychosocialist: “Instead of just using medication, you should treat depression with a balanced regimen of biopsychosocial interventions, including improved diet, better sleep schedule, and helping the patient overcome obstacles in their life.”

  3. The Freudian: “Have you even considered that the patient might be repressing his latent desire to kill his father and marry his mother? Maybe you should analyze him weekly for ten years.”

  4. The Zealot: “Mental illness is caused by separation from Christ/Mohammed/Buddha/Confucius. Your patient should seek forgiveness and let God/Allah/enlightenment/filial piety into their heart/soul/chakras/family.”

  5. The Scientologist: “Psychiatrists are hostile aliens from the planet Farsec. Mental illnesses are caused by body thetans under the influence of the evil overlord Xenu, which can only be removed through dianetics classes, especially the expensive ones.”

In practice, I devote a lot of time and energy to the Colleague and the Biopsychosocialist’s criticisms, a small amount to the Freudian’s, and very little to the Zealot’s and Scientologist’s.

If you portrayed me as a blinkered fanatic who refused to consider other views, I might object by talking about all the time I spent engaging with my colleagues and the biopsychosocialists. Then you could say that those are just loyal opposition within my own modern-20th-century-medicalized-psychiatry paradigm, but, if I’m so broad-minded, why don’t I engage more with Freudians, zealots, and Scientologists? I can only answer that I think those people are wrong. Then you could say “See, , Scott admits that he thinks that his own ideology is the sole source of truth and that outside critics have nothing useful to contribute”.

This is what Eric Raymond calls a Kafkatrap, where any denial is further evidence of guilt. The victim insists “I do so listen to criticism! See, I draw my boundary of who to listen to way out here”, and points to some place very far away from him. The attacker answers “See! Everyone inside that boundary is within your worldview by definition, so you’re admitting that you refuse to listen to criticism from outside your worldview!”

Raymond coined “kafkatrap” during the first round of Social Justice Wars, and this argument figured heavily there. You’re in medicine? You read dozens of books by highly-educated critics of medicine all across the political spectrum? Ah, but have you engaged with this anthroplogist who says medicine is fundamentally racist because surgeons don’t start every operation with a land acknowledgment? Oh, you don’t take her seriously? Seems like you’re one of those insular elitists who think true outsiders, especially black outsiders, have nothing to contribute. If you get my drift, mein Fuhrer.

This is also part of what I was getting at in my plea for effective altruists to stop fawning over their own worst critics. I think rationalists and effective altruists have done a great job engaging with outsiders who have helpful perspectives on things they care about. But the demand - then and now - has always been that we go further. Why aren’t we engaging with the people who think charity is evil? Why aren’t we engaging with the people who think “reason” is a racist scam to claim that white values are objectively correct? Why aren’t we bowing and scraping before the people who spent the past five years saying we were total idiots to worry about AI because it would never be able to count the number of r’s in “strawberry”? Why don’t we worship them as gods? Why don’t we reach out to the people who say we are ugly pervert techbro nerds who should kill themselves, and offer them all-expenses-paid trips to give the keynote speeches at our conferences?

When I try to dialogue with the people who say these things (they’re critics! I have to dialogue with them), I try to ask them what level of “engagement” would make us no longer insular and arrogant and exclusionary - what would allow multiple people in the same social network to share an unpopular belief without getting called “cultish”? I never get a straight answer, and I suspect this is because the real answer would be “You have to abandon all of your unpopular beliefs and switch to believing only popular things instead, and also make me and my friends the high-status leaders of your group”. I decline to do this.

II.

Granting that these people suck, and stepping back from the kafkatrap for a moment, how should we address this epistemic problem? Certainly as a first approximation you shouldn’t spend too much time on people you think are dumb and crazy. But anyone with an opinion sufficiently different from yours probably seems dumb and crazy. If we never listen to anyone whose opinion seems too different from what we currently think is correct, how can we learn?

There’s one very tempting way out: look for “objective evidence” of which critics are worth engaging with. Someone who is very popular and powerful and well-regarded needs to be taken seriously; some marginalized group who can’t get their ideas published in high-impact-factor journals doesn’t. Biopsychosocialists have more social cachet and published journal articles than Scientologists; this accurately predicts that they should be taken more seriously.

But there are two flaws in this plan. First, your perception of “powerful”, “popular”, and “well-regarded” is probably influenced by your current beliefs. I mentioned “high impact-factor journals” above - why do I think those are better “objective” evidence than the number of mentions your ideology gets in Battlefield Earth, one of the best-selling science fiction novels of all time? Probably because I’m a doctor and not a Scientologist.

Second, and more important, it also ensures you always move in a gradient towards Power. Every step you take will be away from your group’s own values, in favor of consensus society. “Abandon everything that makes you unique in favor of being exactly like everyone else” is a Heuristic That Almost Always Works. But it’s also the sort of thing demons whisper to you on desert roads at night. It would be wise to have a plan that tells you something different from the demons.

I rely a little on objective evidence, but I also think it’s healthy to do something like exponential decay: halve the amount of energy you devote to each step away from your current beliefs. If you think medicalized psychiatry is the way to go, you should spend most of your time trying to be the best medicalized psychiatrist you can. Then spend half that amount of time investigating things in the near periphery of medicalized psychiatry, like cognitive therapy and biopsychosocial solutions. Then spend half that amount of time on things in the very far periphery, like Freudianism. Then spend half that amount of time mopping up the things that seem obviously crazy.

“Half” is just an example (I personally do more like a fifth). It doesn’t even have to be the same constant at each step. I think the key idea is that instead of beating yourself up because you don’t read people you hate at exactly the same level as people you respect, you can just read them a little but not too much. This has the advantage of helping you check whether they’re actually as silly as you thought, or whether you were actually missing something important.

(The people trying to kafkatrap you will insist that you didn’t truly understand the few books you read, and that you need to spend years truly soaking yourself in the alternate paradigm before it will can start to seep into someone as beknighted and biased as yourself. This . . . might be true, but there’s no way to spend years investigating every idea, and you shouldn’t award years of your life to whoever can bully you the most, so I still think concentrating on correct-seeming ideas and devoting progressively less energy to progressively more outlandish-seeming ideas - and hoping that this small amount of energy and study will be enough to help you catch the good ones that you should spend more time on - is the way to go.

SSC/ACX book reviews that I consider part of my project of investigating views very different from my own include Just Giving, The Body Keeps The Score, A Future For Socialism, Inventing The Future, Madness And Civilization, Capital In The Twenty-First Century, Seeing Like A State, Unlearn Your Pain, My Brother Ron, Chronicles Of Wasted Time, What’s Wrong With The World, everything I’ve ever written about “neoreaction”, Singer on Marx, San Fransicko, The Others Within Us, I Saw Satan Fall Like Lightning, America Against America, The Cult Of Smart, Sadly Porn, Mussolini On Fascism, and the Frankfurt School.
